[b]July 6, 2028: Aftermath[/b]

Your majesty, you are going to want to see this, Eleonore said, marching into Henri's bedroom with a newspaper in her hand.

What? asked Henri, blinking his eyes as he tried to sit up awake to peer at the paper.

They did it, replied Eleonore, handing him the paper, which he took and read, frowning as he did so.

So they did, he said slowly, before suddenly leaping out of bed, quickly pulling his nightgown down his legs, and donning his slippers, They really did it! he declared giddily as he ran out of the room past a concerned and confused servant. Eleonore merely shrugged and walked out of the room.

After a few minutes, Eleonore found him in his study, speaking with someone rapidly on the phone. Upon seeing her, he put the phone down and said, Ellie, if I can call you that, this is the happiest day of my life, Tears welled up in his eyes, and with a sob, he embraced the president of the state.

Eleonore was unfazed, patting his head and shushing him before he pulled away, wiped the tears from his eyes, and grabbed ahold of her upper arms, Do you know what this means, Eleonore?! he asked.

A very complicated morning? intoned Eleonore, already exasperated. 

Yes! replied Henri, Yes! Yes! Yes!.

Sir, may I remind you, you are still in your bedclothes? she asked, stepping away from the king.

AhI seeOh, I forgot, what morning is it? he asked Eleonore, looking down at his slippers.

Sir, it is the sixth.  Replied Eleonore.

So I havent missed it, I am not dreaming?asked Henri.

How many pills did you take away last night? asked Eleonore.

None, why? asked Henri as he peered out of the window onto the gardens where the palace staff were at work.

Well, youyou stuttered out Eleonore, Never mind, sir, do you expect to address the matter today? she asked.

Why of course, but let me get dressed, and you, you can go to the kitchens, the chef will get you a fine breakfast, replied Henri, rushing out of the room. 

Eleonore had already eaten in the car and wasnt in the mood to descend the four flights of stairs it took to get to the kitchens; however, she decided to do so anyway, unless the king might sour. 

After a while, Henri entered the kitchen, still excited, but seemingly calmed down from his initial waking surprise. Eleonore watched him as he was presented with a croissant and some coffee, suspicious that he might jump up again and spill the coffee over himself.

I do apologise for my earlier conduct, he said, looking at Eleonore, It was unworthy of a man of my stature.

Oh sir, it was no problem, I just ask, that you maintain the amount of sleeping pills you take to just one, joked Eleonore cautiously.

Now, this presents a unique challenge for us, because if thisdeclarationactually gets off the ground, and at this point I am firmly in the belief it will, well, we will probably see the duchy of Belgarde go first, stated Henri.

I have been keeping an eye on the phone, replied Eleonore. However, I doubt that well have the state dissolving overnight, she continued. 

Oh, of course not, thatd be a nightmare, replied Henri.

No, it would, and I expect the Rosenmarkket government to reply in kind she said.

Henri frowned down at his coffee, Should we deploy the gendarme to the border? 

I do not believe that course of action is necessary at the moment, sir, replied Eleonore.

Should we reach out to the local unionist group in Montfleur? I am sure they are aware of this, said Henri.

We can do that, but first we need to calm the legislature. I am sure the national assembly is going to be in a panic today, replied Eleonore.

Henri sighed, Yes, unfortunately,

Well, who would you like to meet first, or well, I guess, summon first, asked Eleonore.

Lets start with the head of the Montfleurois Democratic Union, Jacques Gusteau, and we will go on from there. I believe the MDU will be able to keep the other parties in check, being the centre and all, replied Henri.

Excellent sir, I will get my office to begin calls as well, the sooner we bury any reactionaries, the better off dealing withwhatever the hell this is, will be, replied Eleonore.

[b]Haakon Strømm[/b]

Sir, I regret to inform you that our efforts to halt the production of this petition were fruitless, Intoned General Ramwycke, bowing slightly as he entered the office of Haakon Strømm, who had laid out a map of Rosenmarkke before him.

Where are Kieffe, Stramberg, and sse? asked Haakon in a quiet tone.

They are on their way, replied Ramwycke.

Good.

After a few moments of tense silence, Admiral Kieffe of the Navy, Stramberg of the National Guard, and sse of the air force entered the room, all lining against the wall, and greeting Haakon. 

Gentlemen, intoned Haakon, rising from his seat, Do you know what has happened? 

Sir began sse before being cut off suddenly by Haakon.

It was a rhetoricalquestion, sir, snapped Haakon.

sse gulped as he felt a bead of sweat slide down his forehead, Of course, sir, he replied.

Now, this group has published their manifesto, allegedly, they have evidence, evidence which they received from a foreign source, or so Ramwycke tells me, continued Haakon.

Wewe werent aware of this, sir, stuttered out Stramberg, with a tense smile, giving an accusatory look at Ramwycke.

And yet, here we are, smiled Haakon.

Of course, replied Ramwycke.
But of course, Bjern Randolf will bring it under control, smiled Haakon, the generals suddenly went pale as a silence filled the room, Right? asked Haakon tightly.

UmsirRandolf began sse, referring to the temporary head of the SCSID.

Randolf was compromised, followed Ramwycke, with a frown.

Silence hit the room like a bullet, Haakon leaned back, his hands trembling as he rubbed one across his snout, clearing his throat he leaned forward once more, That was an order! he  Xshouted, slamming his pointer finger into the map, Randolf was supposed to bring them to order! he shouted. Who the hell do you think you are! To allow yourself to be compromised in such a manner! he paused as he stood, withdrawing a ruler from the desk.

The generals looked down with embarrassment visibly shaken by the outburst.

Is this what it has come to? My own forces, lying to me? continued Haakon, Everyone has been lying to me! he shouted, shaking his finger at the generals, Our leaders, our generals, our spies, are all contemptable, cowards, disloyal to the very blood that flows through their putrid rotting bodies! he declared, throwing the ruler across the room.

Sir, please, pleaded Ramwycke, however Haakon wasnt done.

Please what? They are cowards, failures, traitors! declared Haakon, These leaders, these spies, these are the scum of the Rosenmarkket people! You are the scum with them! he pointed at the generals, You! YOU! YOU! he paused to dab a towel over his head before continuing, They spend years in the academie, and for what? To learn how to write with a ballpoint pen! he continued, Failures, miserable cowards, I shouldve had you all shot! BANG! BANG! BANG! ALL DEAD! he screamed, sitting down once more. 

And yet, I have defeated the Wuloosyans, myself I have done so! he declared beating his chest proudly.

No, no, I would rather die with Rosenmarkke than surrender to the frauds in Montfleur, he continued, leaning over in his chair and staring at his shoes, You may go, I have nothing else, he said as the generals shuffled out of the room, shaken.

[b]On Tables and Nations[/b]

There are a variety of tables in the world, spanning from low tables to tall tables, from tables wherein you put your tea to tables where you set your coffee. There are oak tables, mahogany tables, plastic tables (terribly cheap things), and glass tables. 

Of course, each table has its own assortment of legs, however the standard table has four legs, and without one, the table cannot stand. It is in this manner that a table and a nation are similar.

Within a country, four major things are needed to keep the country standing, chiefly: unity, liberty, good governance, and economic growth. It is of these which Rosenmarkke has none of these things.

And indeed, what is a table without legs? It is merely a plank. A useless piece of wood only useful but to become a table.

At this moment, Rosenmarkke is a piece of wood, and indeed, there is left not one sane man or woman who can make this country some legs, primarily because they have shied away from the duties and outed themselves as cowards.

But, as the petition of grievances is released, the general public has awakened to the reality of where Rosenmarkke stands, and eagerly awaits the answer to the issues, mobilising themselves to make Rosenmarkke great again.

It is this adage which we shall adopt in pursuing the unification between Rosenmarkke and Montfleur, our goal is not to merely reform Rosenmarkke but to make it great once more. And it is through unification that we can ensure this.

Montfleur and Rosenmarkke shall build a new table and upon it a lace tablecloth, and a new family shall be built of the likes which the world hasnt seen since the 1600s. 

  - John Crockery (Head of the Carpentry Union of Rosenmarkke)

[b]July 7, 2028: A meeting with the parties[/b]

Good afternoon madames and sirs, began Henri as he walked into the conference room in the palais des populaires, the home of the National Assembly of Montfleur.

The heads of the political parties of Montfleur were seated around the table, all rose and greeted the king politely.

Sit, sit,  stated the king as he sat himself down at the head of the table, Now, as you know Rosenmarkke is on the brink of collapse, he stated, I hold that we cannot permit this situation to go on, 

Jean Rousemond head of the communist party of Montfleur coughed slightly and then spoke, Your majesty, your suggestion of reunification is rash, uncalled for, and it would require a massive political shift, 

Mr. Rousemond, at this moment, reunification is not my primary goal, it is what do we do with the collapsing state on our borders, I have already gotten a letter from the duc of Belgarde, requesting aide in the event of an escalation, replied Henri.

A murmur ran around the room.

But I mean the duc of Belgarde has a right to do so, the act of settlement never recognised Rosenmarkkes claim on the southern half of the duchy, intoned Rolande Perot head of the Blue Union.

Another murmur.

So what are we talking about here your majesty, military action? A firm declaration? Anything we do will break neutrality, replied Rousemond.

Mr. Chairman, intoned Perot, Has it perhaps struck the left coalition, that neutrality is rapidly becoming an impossible thing at this moment in time?

Henri nodded, Mr. Perot makes a point, Haakon Strømm is reportedly considering actions to allegedly stabilise the country, including actions which violate international law, neutrality is rapidly becoming a non solution,

Violate international law? Scoffed Rousemond, Do you mean he intends to invade?

I believe he does, in an effort to boost his regime, he might attempt a false flag operation and attempt to invade Montfleur, accuse us of aligning with the Wuloosyan government against Rosenmarkke during the war that happened earlier this year, replied Henri.

What is the situation on the ground? Asked Rousemond.

The petition has given local popular movements some backbone, but right now they arent generally unified, if we do take action, we need a unified movement, said Henri.

Alright, Rousemond nodded.

Now has anyone read the petition? Asked Henri.

The leaders all nodded in the affirmative.

Good, I intend to bring this matter to the International Court of Justice, began Henri, This will work to further destabilize the regime, and expose the crimes that were committed by the  government, 

Sir, are you sure? Asked Perot.

More than sure, and regardless of when it happens, I want to see the government of Rosenmarkke on the stand of a military tribunal before the world, replied Henri firmly.

Well, I cannot deny that the actions of Rosenmarkke over the past fifty years have been irrational, I think we should reach out to their organization, THEP, and get the other nations to move to remove Rosenmarkke from it, replied Rousemond.

We can direct the office of foreign affairs to look into it, replied Henri.

I think these are the best actions right now, replied Perot, I do not object, he added.

Very well then, gentlemen, prepare your parties to vote on the matter of neutrality, for we are about to cross the Rouen river with this one, replied Henri standing, And once we do, we shall not turn back,
